prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Trailing her father, bearing his hand axe, the girl thought she had never guessed what earthly majesty was before then, as he strode unconcernedly holding a vicious gander by the horny mitts and let the big wings batter his knees. She was also surprised to feel a liberating satisfaction in the coming bloodshed, and that notwithstanding all the times she had been beleaguered and had fled, today she did not fear the barnyard hubub. Yet, as her father’s clever stroke fell, as the pronged head skipped sideways and the neck plumes stiffened with blood from the cleft, she was angry; and, when the headless goose ran to the brook and was carried off into the woods alive, she rejoiced, and subsequently frequented those woods and avoided her father. When the goose began to mend she brought him small hominy, which was welcome though she had to press the kernels one by one into the pink neck that throbbed into her palm; when haemorrhage occurred she would not spare handkerchiefs, and stanching the spot she felt a thrill of sympathy. But for the most part there was steady progress, and growing vigor was accompanied by restlessness, and one cool day the blind thing was batted out of existence by a motorcycle. She had no time for tears. She ran upstairs to miss her father’s barytone commiseration, then out onto the fields, and, holding an old red pinwheel, ran ran ran ran.

outputs.L2: Walking behind her father and carrying his hatchet, the girl realized she had never before understood what worldly grandeur could mean, watching him march along casually, gripping a savage gander by its leathery feet while its enormous wings hammered against his legs. She was equally astonished to discover a sense of freeing contentment in the slaughter to come, and to notice that despite all the occasions she had been cornered and had run away, on this day the racket of the barnyard held no terror for her. And yet, when her father's skillful blow landed, when the horned head bounced to one side and the feathers around the neck grew rigid with blood from the wound, she felt fury; and when the beheaded bird dashed to the stream and was swept off into the forest still living, she was overjoyed, and afterward began haunting that forest while keeping her distance from her father. As the goose started to recover, she carried him bits of hominy, which he accepted gladly even though she had to push the grains individually into the pink throat that pulsed against her hand; whenever bleeding happened she wouldn't hold back her handkerchiefs, and pressing them to the wound she experienced a rush of compassion. Still, for the most part he improved steadily, and his returning strength came paired with a growing agitation, until one chilly day the sightless creature was struck out of life by a motorcycle. She allowed herself no moment for weeping. She dashed upstairs to escape the deep tones of her father's sympathy, then out into the meadows, and, clutching a faded red pinwheel, ran ran ran ran.
outputs.L3:
# The Gander

The girl trailed after her father as he made his way toward the pen, and though she could not have named the feeling, there was something in his broad-shouldered stride that struck her as majestic. He moved with the calm authority of a man who knew exactly what he meant to do. The gander waited in its enclosure, and she found herself thrilling with a strange satisfaction at the thought of the blood that was soon to come, as if the promise of that violence were a kind of ceremony she had been invited to witness.

But when the moment arrived—when her father's arm came down and the killing stroke fell—something turned over inside her. The satisfaction curdled into anger, sudden and hot, rising in her throat before she could understand it. And then the impossible happened: the goose, headless and streaming, tore free of his grip and lurched away, half-flying, half-stumbling, into the dark line of the woods. She felt her heart leap. She wanted to cheer. That the ruined creature should escape, should refuse to die, seemed to her the most triumphant thing she had ever seen.

In the days that followed, she kept her secret carefully. She found the wounded bird and took it upon herself to bring it back to life, hiding it away and tending it with a devotion she had never given anything before. She fed it hominy, one kernel at a time, coaxing it to eat, and when the wound wept she pressed it and stanched the bleeding with her own hands, feeling each time a shiver of sympathy so keen it was almost pleasure. Slowly the goose mended. Its strength returned, and with it a restlessness—a wildness that made it pace and stir and strain against the small world she had made for it.

Then, on a cool bright day, it was over in an instant. A motorcycle passed along the road, and the goose that had survived the axe, that she had nursed back from the very edge, was struck dead in a single careless moment.

She could not cry. Not in front of anyone. When her father came to her, reaching out with soft words meant to comfort, she twisted away from him and ran. She fled across the yard and out into the open fields, and in her hand she clutched an old red pinwheel, its faded blades spinning and spinning in the rushing air as she went, carrying her grief where no one could follow.
outputs.L4:
# The Pinwheel

The morning my father asked me to help him with the goose, the frost still clung to the grass in silver patches that crunched beneath our boots. I was eight years old, and I had never watched anything die before.

"Hold the basin steady, Marta," he said, his voice as ordinary as if he'd asked me to pass the salt at supper.

I nodded because I could not find words. The goose was a fat gray thing we had raised through the summer, and though my mother insisted we never name the animals we intended to eat, I had secretly called her Frau Weber, after our stern neighbor whose feathers seemed always ruffled.

My father laid the goose across the block. His hands were sure and gentle, the same hands that carried me to bed when I fell asleep by the fire. The axe came down. I looked away, and when I looked back, the head lay separate in the dirt, its black eye already dulling.

But then the body moved.

Not the twitching my father had warned me about—the last confusion of the nerves. The goose *stood up*. It rose from the block, headless and impossible, and staggered three steps across the yard before collapsing against the fence.

"It's nothing," my father said. "Just the body. It doesn't feel anything."

Yet something rose in me that I could not name—a fury so sudden and enormous that my whole body shook with it. How dare it live like this? How dare he? I hated my father in that moment, hated the axe, hated the frost and the ordinary morning and myself for holding the basin. And beneath the anger, welling up like water from a spring, came a pity so tender it hurt to breathe.

That night, while my parents slept, I crept to the yard.

The goose was still alive.

I do not know how. Perhaps my father's aim had spared some secret cord of life. I gathered the terrible, breathing body into my arms, feeling the heartbeat still fluttering beneath the feathers, and I carried it into the woods where the old woodcutter's shed stood abandoned.

For eleven days I nursed it. I brought mashed grain softened with milk, dribbling it into the ruined place where a head should be, coaxing life into a thing that had every reason to surrender it. And—God help me—it grew stronger. It learned to find the food by feel. It followed the sound of my voice, turning its blind, headless body toward me when I came through the trees.

I told no one. This was my secret rebellion against the natural order, my proof that love could stitch back together what an axe had torn apart.

On the twelfth day, I came to the shed and the goose was gone.

I found it on the road that ran along the forest's edge. A motorcycle had passed—I never learned whose—and the goose that had survived the impossible had not survived the ordinary. It lay in the dust, finally and completely dead, and this time there was no mistaking it.

My father found me there. He must have followed me, must have known all along about the shed, the grain, the secret. He knelt beside me in the road and reached out to gather me the way he'd gathered the goose that first morning.

"Marta," he said softly. "Liebling. I'm sorry. Come here now."

But I could not bear his gentleness. I could not bear that he had been right—that the body always dies, that love changes nothing, that I had only prolonged a suffering I mistook for hope. I twisted away from his open arms.

In my pocket was the pinwheel he had bought me at the spring fair, red and yellow and blue. I pulled it out and ran.

I ran into the wide fields where the wind came cold and clean off the mountains, and I held the pinwheel high above my head so that it spun and spun, a blur of color against the pale enormous sky. I ran until my lungs burned, until my father's voice faded behind me, until there was nothing but the whir of the little wheel and the thunder of my own heart.

I was not trying to fly the pinwheel. I was trying to outrun the thing inside me—the grief that had no bottom, the knowledge that had come too early. I ran as though I could leave my sorrow standing in the field behind me, a small dark shape growing smaller, while I disappeared into the wind and the turning colors and the enormous, indifferent light.

But grief, I would learn, is faster than any child. It runs alongside you. It waits at the edge of the field. And it is always, always there when at last you have to stop.
outputs.L5:
# Trailing Behind

She walked slowly through the garden, her fingers trailing along the tops of the tall grasses that swayed in the afternoon breeze. Each blade left a whisper against her palm, a gentle reminder that she was not alone in this quiet space.

She had come here often as a child, chasing butterflies and dreams that seemed endless back then. Now, years later, the paths felt smaller, the distances shorter. Yet something about this place still held the same magic it always had.

The ivy climbed the old stone wall, its tendrils trailing downward like green rivers frozen in time. She paused to admire how nature reclaimed what people abandoned, patient and persistent in its quiet work.

Life had not turned out the way she planned. There had been disappointments, wrong turns, moments when giving up seemed like the easiest choice. Yet here she stood, still breathing, still hoping, still moving forward one careful step at a time.

She looked back at the trail of footprints she had left in the soft earth behind her. They marked where she had been, but they did not dictate where she would go. Every path forward remained hers to choose.

The sun began its slow descent, painting the sky in shades of amber and rose. She lingered a moment longer, unwilling to leave just yet. Some places deserved to be savored, and some feelings deserved to be felt fully before letting them go.

With a final glance at the trailing vines and the golden light, she turned toward home, carrying the peace of the garden with her. Tomorrow would bring new challenges, yet tonight, she felt ready for whatever came next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, literary flash-fiction piece about a girl who tries to save a goose after her father beheads it for slaughter, ending in the goose's accidental death. Use dense, old-fashioned prose.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Mercy of Small Hands

The girl was seven that autumn, and did not yet know that some kindnesses are only crueler deaths dressed in the garments of hope.

Her father took the axe to the block in the grey hour before the frost had lifted, and the goose—that great white indignation of a bird, who had chased her through the yard all summer and nipped the tender flesh behind her knees—went to its end with a single stroke. The head fell into the wet leaves. The body did not know it. This was the thing she could not have imagined: how the body reared up from her father's loosened grip and ran, wings thrashing the air into white confusion, blood ribboning behind it like the tail of some terrible comet.

"Leave it," her father said. "It's the nerves only. It'll drop."

But she did not leave it. She saw the thing she loved and hated running blind and headless through the cabbage rows, and something in her small chest broke open like an egg, and she thought—with the whole fierce foolishness of childhood—that she might yet gather it up and hold the pieces of it together and make it live.

She ran after it through the cold garden. She caught it at last against the fence, the body still warm, still surging, and she pressed it to her nightgown and felt the animal engine of it laboring against her ribs. She held the stump of its neck as though her palm might be a poultice against the fact of the axe. She whispered to it. She told it she was sorry. She told it to be still.

And in her holding—in the desperate cradling of her arms that meant only love, only the wish to spare—she pressed too hard, or turned it wrong, or the last thread that bound the living to the dead was severed by her very tenderness. The body shuddered once, enormously, and then was only meat.

She stood a long while with it cooling in her arms.

Her father came and took the ruined thing from her without a word, for what word was there. And the girl understood, in the marrow of her, a lesson older than the frost: that she had wanted to be the hand that healed, and had been instead the hand that finished; that mercy, held too tight, becomes the thing it fled; and that we are none of us, not even the small and blameless, wholly innocent of the deaths we mean to prevent.

She did not weep. She had passed beyond it, into that cold country where the very young sometimes go, and from which they return already a little older, carrying the first true weight of the world in their two clean, unwashable hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single dark, lyrical paragraph exploring a child's complicated feelings about violence, mercy, and her father, centered on a barnyard scene.
counterfactuals.output: The rooster came at me sideways every morning, spurs like little knives, and I hated him with the clean hatred only a child can hold, the kind that doesn't know yet how heavy hatred gets. My father caught him one gray dawn, and I remember thinking *good, finally,* remember the ugly leap of gladness in my chest when he pinned those thrashing wings against the chopping block. But then his hands went still. He looked at that mean bird a long moment, and something in his face folded inward like a door closing on a room I'd never see, and he let it go. Watched it stagger, indignant, back into the yellow dust. *Even the wicked ones,* he said, not to me, not to anyone, and I have spent the rest of my life trying to understand whether that was weakness or the largest mercy I have ever witnessed, whether the softness in a man's hands is the same softness that lets the world's small cruelties strut free—and whether, when he looked at me across that block, he was deciding something too, whether I was the rooster or the knife, and whether he had ever, in the long dark arithmetic of loving a difficult thing, been tempted to bring the blade down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a story in the style of early 20th-century American literary fiction about a farm girl who nurses a decapitated-but-living goose back to health, only for it to die again.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Gander

The frost had come early that year, silvering the fields of the Hendricks farm before October was rightly finished, and it was on such a morning that Alma found the gander.

She was fourteen and built lean as a fence rail, with hair the color of winter wheat and hands already roughened by the work that fell to a farm girl whose mother had died and whose father spoke perhaps a dozen words between sunup and supper. The chores did not care about grief. The cows wanted milking whether or not a woman lay beneath the churchyard elm, and the chickens wanted feeding, and the great white geese that her mother had prized wanted their corn scattered in the yard.

It was Halloran, the hired man, who had done it. He was not a cruel man, only a careless one, and when he swung the hatchet at the block that morning he had been thinking of other things—of the girl in town, perhaps, or of the wages he was owed. The blade came down and the head sprang loose into the wet grass, and the body, which by all the laws Alma understood should have surrendered at once, did not.

It rose up.

It flapped its enormous wings and staggered across the yard, blood spotting the frost like a terrible sowing, and Halloran cursed and crossed himself and let it run. Alma, coming from the henhouse with her apron full of eggs, saw the thing lurch toward her, headless and yet somehow living, and she did not scream. She had seen death before. This was not quite death, and that was worse, and it caught her by the throat in a way that dying never had.

"Let it be," Halloran said. "It'll drop directly."

But it did not drop. By noon it stood trembling by the woodpile, and by evening it had folded itself into the lee of the barn, and Alma, who could not have said why, brought it water in a shallow pan.

She learned, in the days that followed, the strange mechanics of the thing. The hatchet had taken the head but spared some portion of the neck and its workings, so that a red passage remained by which the creature might be fed. She mixed cornmeal with milk into a gruel and coaxed it down that raw pipe with the patience of one who has nothing else in all the world to spend patience on. She bound the wound with rags boiled clean. She kept it in a box by the kitchen stove, against her father's grumbling, and in the night she rose to tend it as her mother must once have risen to tend her.

"It's not natural," her father said. He stood in the doorway with the lamp throwing his shadow long across the floor. "A thing like that. You'd do better to wring what's left of its neck."

"It wants to live," Alma said.

Her father looked at her a long moment. Something moved behind his weathered face, some old sorrow surfacing like a fish and sinking again before it could be named. "Wanting," he said, "is not the same as living," and he went up to his cold bed.

But the gander lived. That was the wonder of it, the thing the neighbors came to see when word got round, driving their wagons up the frozen lane to stand in the yard and marvel. It lived, and more than lived—it grew strong, its body filling out again, its white feathers regaining their gloss. It knew Alma's step. When she came into the kitchen of a morning it would stir in its box and lift the ruined stump of its neck toward the sound of her, and though it had no eyes to see her nor any voice to call, she understood that it was glad.

She loved it the way the lonely love, which is to say entirely and without reservation, pouring into that broken vessel all the tenderness she had no other place to put. She named it nothing. To name it would have been to admit it was only a goose, and it had become to her something larger—a proof, perhaps, that a thing could be broken past all sense and mending and still refuse to die. She needed that proof. She held it against the winter and against the silence of her father and against the small stone in the churchyard, and it kept.

For six weeks it kept.

Then one morning in the deep of December she came down and found it lying still. It had not toppled from its box; it had simply stopped, sometime in the dark hours, as quietly as a candle gutters when the wax is spent. She knelt beside it and put her hand upon the cold white breast and felt no flutter there, and she understood that the wound had never truly healed at all—that some slow poison had been working in it the whole while, some rot too deep for boiled rags and cornmeal gruel, and that all her nursing had bought was time, and not even very much of that.

She did not cry at first. She sat on the cold kitchen floor with the dead gander in her lap and looked at the gray light coming up in the window, and she thought about her mother, whom she had also nursed, in her fashion, bringing broth to the sickroom and holding the thin hand and believing, because she was a child and had to believe it, that love was a thing that could keep another creature in the world.

It could not. She knew that now with a completeness that no one had been able to teach her, that she had needed to learn with her own hands upon a cooling body. Love was only love. It was not a rope you could throw to the drowning. You could pour it out entire and it would not weigh, in the end, against an ounce of the world's blind insistence on taking back what it had made.

Her father found her there when he came down. He stood in the doorway a moment, and then, for the first time since the burying, he crossed the room and lowered himself to the floor beside her, his old knees cracking, and he put his rough arm around his daughter's shaking shoulders, and the two of them sat together in the pale light with the dead thing between them, and neither of them said a word, because there was nothing that words could do, and they had both of them at last stopped believing there was.

Outside, the snow began, small and dry and patient, filling up the yard where the blood had been, covering the block and the frozen furrows and the long lane down to the road, laying its clean white indifference over the whole of the waiting earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a piece of experimental short prose (one paragraph) that begins with a girl following her father to kill a gander and ends with her running across a field holding a pinwheel.
counterfactuals.output: She followed him out past the woodpile, past the place where the dog was buried, her father's boots pressing crescents into the frost and she fitting her smaller feet inside them, and the gander was somewhere down by the pond making its ugly trumpet, the sound that had chased her all summer, that had bitten the meat of her calf and left a bruise the color of a plum, and now here was the hatchet swinging loose in his fist like a second, longer hand, and she thought: *good, good, kill it,* and then she thought nothing, because the morning was doing that thing where everything goes very bright and very still, the reeds standing up like they'd been told to, and the gander came around the shed white as a bedsheet, white as the thing you wave when you give up, and it did not give up, it lowered its head and hissed and she saw in its flat orange eye a small girl and a large man reflected upside down and getting closer, and her father raised his arm, and she wanted to watch and she could not watch, and somewhere in the not-watching she was already turning, already a body in motion, and the shriek that came was hers or the bird's or the two of them braided together forever now, and she was gone, across the field, through the wet grass slapping her shins, and in her hand—she didn't remember picking it up, it had been staked at the garden's edge all season—the little tin pinwheel spun and spun and spun, feeding on her running, throwing off light, saying nothing, meaning nothing, going faster the faster she fled, a small bright wheel of wind she was making all by herself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write flash fiction about childhood, cruelty, and grief on a farm, using rich vocabulary and an ambiguous, unsettling tone.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Feathers

The bantam hen we called Duchess laid eggs the color of old teeth, and Grandmother said this meant she was rotting from the inside, the way certain apples brown at the core while the skin stays taut and rosy. I was seven that summer, learning the arithmetic of the farm: how many chicks survived the fox, how many teats a sow could feed, how thin the line ran between the living and the meat.

My brother Cole was eleven and had discovered that cruelty could be a kind of tenderness, or its inverse—I never quite parsed which. He collected the barn cats' offspring and held them underwater in the rain barrel with a patience I found almost devotional, his lips moving as though in prayer, counting. Afterward he wept, genuinely, snot-slick and shuddering, then buried each one beneath the elm with small crosses fashioned from popsicle sticks. He mourned what he murdered. This seemed to me, even then, a terrible and honest thing.

The summer my mother left—walked the gravel drive with a suitcase and did not look back, her figure diminishing until the heat-shimmer swallowed her whole—Cole stopped burying things. He simply left them where they fell.

I found Duchess in the tall grass by the fence line, her feathers dispersed in a wide corona, the down still lifting on the breeze as though she might reassemble herself and strut away. Something had opened her. I understood, with the sudden clarity children sometimes possess, that Cole had done this, and that he had not wept, and that this was the more frightening thing—not the violence but its aftermath of silence, the absence where grief should have lived.

I gathered her feathers into my apron. They weighed nothing. I thought of my mother's hands, how they too had weighed nothing when they cupped my face those final mornings, already halfway to elsewhere.

That night Cole came into my room and lay beside me in the dark, smelling of iron and hay, and whispered that he was sorry, though he did not say for what. I did not answer. Outside, the surviving hens muttered in their sleep, and the elm held its small crosses like a mouth holding teeth it could not bring itself to swallow.

In the morning the eggs were white as bone. I ate them anyway. We ate everything that summer. We were always, always hungry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
